section.p: Malleus Deum is a player-facing game. We try and make the players do all the rolling. So when a PC is attacked by an NPC the player makes a defence check against the NPCs attack DC. When a PC attacks an NPC the player makes an attack check against the NPCs defence DC. When one PC attacks another PC both players roll, the first PC makes an attack check, the second PC makes a defence check.

playexample.p: Dourli attacks a preternaturally large rat. He uses his Axe Strike 2 ability against the rats defensive DC of 13. He rolls an outcome of 12 with the additional +2 for ranks in Axe Strike he gets a 14 which hits, since it's greater than rats defensive DC. The rat takes the standard axe damage to its hit points.

Then it is the rats turn to attack. The rat uses its bite attack which has a DC of 15. Dourli uses Shield Block 3 to defend himself (using his reaction). Dourli rolls another 12 then adds 3 for his rank in Shield Block to get a total of 15. He successfully blocks the attack and takes no damage.

section.p:
Combat Groups
Groups Combat
Combat is a core part of the game and has its own specific set of rules. Before combat starts all the combatants are divided into groups by the GM, typically there will be be one group of PCs, and one to three groups of monsters/NPCs.

Initiative Order
Group Order
Malleus Deum uses Group Order to determine the order in which these Groups act during combat. When a Group acts, every member of the group takes a turn. Members of the group may take their turns in any order within their group. So when the PC's group acts, the players may choose the order in which their characters act, within their group, or just take their turns in clockwise order around the table. Once all members of a group have taken their turn, the next group in order acts.

subsection.p: In mundane combat encounters the GM should just choose the Group Order. If the monsters start the fight then perhaps they should have initiative. Otherwise the GM should consider just allowing the PCs to go first, they are supposed to be the heroes after all. This makes combat faster, keeps the game moving and gives the PCs agency.
If the GM wishes one of a number of different checks may be used before combat to determine group order. These checks are: Initiative, Surprise, and Ambush.

subsubsection.p:
The GM should consider getting the players to make an initiative check in any of the following circumstances:
The narrative dictates, when confronting "boss" monsters, or
When the stakes are high, when inititiative order might be strategically important to the outome of the combat, or
To punish the PCs for poor strategic decisions, or
To punish the PCs for bad luck when executing their plans.

Initiative Check Initiative is an Opposed Group Delegate check. One member of each group is chosen by the GM to roll an ability check to determine their groups Initiative Result. During combat the groups act in order from highest initiative result to lowest..

An Initiative Check is made using an ability chosen by the GM, and based on context. Some abilities that could be used to make the initiative check are Perception, Speed, Listen, and Scout. We use the term Initiative Check to refer to this check irrespective of what underlying ability was used to make the check. Different groups may use different abilities for an Initiative Check.

sec:surprise Surprise Under certain circumstances it is possible for one group to surprise another group. For this to happen two conditions must be satisfied:
The GM rules that Surprise is possible, and
One group must succeed at a Surprise Check

The GM should rule that surprise is possible when the situation and narrative allow it. For example it may be impossible for one group to surprise another on barren plains where there is no cover for miles around, or when two groups approach each other down a light corridor. The GM should ensure that it is very hard to surprise groups expecting to be attacked.
A Surprise Check is a Group Delegate Check where one character from the surprising group checks their Stealth Result versus one of their opponents Perception or Listen Check Result.

p.emph: When a group is surprised it gets no actions for the first round of combat. In addition the surprised group must make a Mettle Check. The attackers gain advantage on any Checks during a Surprise Roll. Additionally, whether the surprise attempt is successful or not the would be surpriser automatically wins initiative.

playexample.p: Dourli, attempts to surprise two gang members in the city by attacking them from behind under the cover of darkness. Dourli is aware of his opponents already, but do the gang members become aware of Dourli? Dourli makes a Stealth check against his opponents Perception DC. If successful his opponents will be unaware of him and he will surprise the gang members, if he fails to surprise them he probably should still go first in the initiative, since he is a player character and he initiated the attack.

subsubsection.p: Ambush Ambush is special subtype of Surprise that occurs when the ambusher has enough time to plan their initial attack well. For a successful ambush one group must be be stationary waiting in ambush. The other group must move into the ambush area.

p.emph: Players receive a +6 modifier to their surprise when ambushing, and they receive a -6 modifier to their surprise roll when being ambushed. The effects of being ambushed are the same as those for being surprised. In addition, the ambushers may have had time to set traps and snares, prepare actions, cast non-combat spells at the GMs discretion.

section.p: Because Malleus Deum has to describe events over a range of time frames, such as minutes for negotiation and exploration, and hours or days for travel, we usually take a fairly informal approach to time-keeping in the game for these activities. However, because combat is very important in the game and because we want action in combat to have high fidelity, combat gets its own particulary time scale in the game.
Combat rounds represent about ten seconds of time in-game. During a round every participant in the combat takes a single Turn.

Actions Standard Action Move Action Minor Action In a characters Turn the character has time to perform a Standard Action, a Move Action and a Minor Action. Actions can be demoted from a Standard Action to a Move or Minor Action, and from a Move Action to a Minor Action. These actions can be performed in any order within a combat round and they are all optional.
There are a few extra complications to combat: Immediate Actions, Out of Turn Actions, Reactions and Interrupts, Free Actions, Miscellaneous Actions, and Prepared Actions which we discuss later.

subsection.p: Standard actions are the main combat actions that are used for most physical attacks and many spells. Examples are Sword Strike and Axe Strike.

During combat there are a number of different movement actions available. A normal Move Action allows the character to move their normal move distance. A Run Action is performing two Move Actions in a Round, the character Moves and then demotes their Standard Action to another Move Action, moving twice.
The character may Flee which is a Run Action away from danger. Fleeing characters gain an extra d6 movement, but must make a Morale Check to stop fleeing.

Characters may also make a Charge Action. In order to make a charge a character has to be greater than their movement away from the target of their charge. First the charging character moves their movement towards their opponent. Then the Charging character must make a Mettle Check. If they fail, they make an additional move towards their opponent but do not attack. If they succeed they move an additional movement, with a +d6 bonus movement, and may then perform a melee attack.
On a grid, the distance the character may move a number of squares up to the movement value on their character sheet. Using TOTM the GM will dictate distances to the players.
A minor action is any operation that can be performed in very short period of time, grabbing an item from your belt, opening a door, picking an item up .
A Free Action is an optional extra action that the character performs in his turn and that does not count against their limit of actions for their round.

Immediate Actions are Free Actions that the characters can perform once, at any time during the round. Examples of Immediate Actions are using Leadership to try and cause a halt to combat to allow negotiation, and Fleeing.
Some tasks require longer than a standard action to perform, typically either one or more whole turns. We call these full-turn or multi-turn actions.

A Full Turn Action takes a whole turn to complete. That is one standard action, one move action and one minor action. These actions can be performed in any order and they can be started in one turn and finished in another. Multi Turn Actions require some number of full turn actions. For example, a Two-Turn Action requires two standard actions, two move actions and two minor actions to complete.

Collective actions allow multiple characters to contribute actions towards a goal. In these cases all characters that contribute must have the appropriate ability. The character that contributes the last required action rolls for the check. Collective actions should have the collective keyword.

Long Actions may or may not be interuptable. If an action is interuptable characters can perform some part of the action, then do something else, and the return to the action and continue performing the action without losing previous progress. If an action is not interuptable then any interuption will cause the action to fail and any progress will be lost.
Under certain circumstances a character will be able to perform an additional Out of Turn Action during someone else's action or when a special triggering event occurs.
Usually, a character can perform at most one Out of Turn Action per round.

Out of Turn Actions are any actions that the GM deems may be performed as an Out-of-Turn Action due to some special circumstance, or any action specially tagged as such, Shield Block, Sword Parry, Cloak Fighting and Dodge.
If two or more characters want to perform Out-of-Turn Actions at the same time then the order in which those actions are performed is determined by the GM.

Miscellaneous actions refer to things that characters do during combat for which no explicit rules exist, reading the runes that close a magic portal, releasing a portcullis, mounting a horse, quaffing a potion, pushing a load of barrels over and so on.

For many miscellaneous actions the GM will just have to make a ruling as to the check required and the type of action; standard, move or minor: as it would infeasible for us to provide rules for the myriad of miscellaneous actions that might occur. We suggest that the GM rule that these are minor actions if they can as it encourages strategic thinking and more variety during combat. You could estimate the time required and work out the actions required as follows.. whole turn is 10 seconds, a standard action is six seconds, a move action is three seconds, and a minor action is one second. Then, if an action will take thirty seconds to perform it will need three whole rounds to complete.

If the character knows that a combat is imminent they may declare that they prepare an action. At that point, at the GMs discretion, the action gains a +3 check modifier, a prepared arrow shot triggered when someone enters a room would gain a +3 bonus to succeed.

Since combat is such a major part of the game the characters will be rolling Boons and Banes quite often. The standard Boon for martial abilities is double damage. The standard Bane for martial abilities is half damage.
Some suggested boons and banes for use during combat checks can be found in Tables table:{{ doc_name }}-defence-fumble and table:{{ doc_name }}-attack-fumble in the appendix.

playexample.p: The thugs have returned to the cellars. Dourli and Roslyn have been unable to escape and now a fight looks inevitable. It's still dark and our heroes have managed to hide from the thugs so far. Dourli attacks the thugs from his hidden position attempting to ambush them. The GM notes that the Thugs will be expecting trouble, they are Alert, and so decides the bonus to ambush the thugs is reduced to +3.

Dourli tries to get advantage from the dark keyword of the cellars and prepares an attack. The GM agrees and gives the adventurers a +1 arguing that the fact that the thugs were expecting to find Dourli down here would somewhat negate that advantage. Dourli agrees.

As this is a group delegate check the GM chooses Roslyn to check her Stealth versus the thugs Perception DC. If Roslyn succeeds then the Thugs are ambushed, Roslyn and Dourli win initiative and get a free round of attacks, the first attack from Dourli gains a bonus to succeed as a prepared action and the thugs must make a morale check.

Dourli and his ally Roslyn, have been cornered by the local gang leader Fenton One-Eye and two of his thugs. A fight in the cellar of the Inn has been underway for some number of rounds. During the fight a few kegs of whisky have been smashed and there is a shallow pool of whisky on the ground.

One of the thugs attacks Dourli with an Axe Strike I. Dourli defends with a Shield Block 3, since he has rank 3 so he rolls 2D12 with a +3 bonus to his block, the attack has a DC of 13 + 1 for the Axe Strike rank. He needs an 11 or more on his roll to succeed. He roll double fours. That is a failure and also a boon. The GM declares that Dourli takes half damage which for an axe is 3 hit points. That has used Dourlis one Out-of-Turn action for the round.
The second thug tries to stab Dourli with his dagger. Dourli has no Out-of-Turn Actions left so he has to defend with an Armour save.

section.subsection:
Grids vs Theatre of the Mind
Movement MovementGrids MovementTOTM Grids Theatre of the the mind (TOTM) TOTM (Theatre of the the mind) Combat may either be performed either, formally, using a map Grid with miniatures or tokens, or narratively/informally using the Theatre of the Mind, TOTM.
MovementStandard Grid Size (3m/10feet diameter) If the combat takes place on a grid then the map determines the distances for movement, spell area of effect, missile weapon range etc. The standard scale maps in this game squares or hexes are 3 meters or 10' in diameter.
FIXME... On a map a run is simply a double movement, a charge is a movement + d6 extra squares then an attack if the enemy is in range. Fleeing characters move twice their movement rate +d6 extra squares.
Movement is halved over difficult terrain. Difficult terrain includes: muddy ground, rocky ground, and generally any terrain with a lot of debris, brambles etc.
Range
Range Long Range Range, Long (-3)
Missile weapons and some spells are ranged actions.
Up to that range the action is made without any modifiers. If the ability or weapon has two ranges then the first is the range at which no range modifiers apply. The second range is long range for that ability or weapon and the check suffers a -3 check modifier. If the ability has no second range specified then the ability or weapon cannot be used at a range greater than the one specified and attempts to do so automatically fail.

Cover
Cover Cover provides modifiers to checks for most missile weapons and for melee combat. Light Cover afforded by bushes and the like gives a one shift modifier, Hard Cover, such as a half wall, provides a two shift modifier. Full Cover provides a three shift modifier. The GM should feel free to choose a check modifier that fits the cover available to the characters.
FIXME: Characters provide cover for allies behind them. Shield extra shift, Large extra shift, Small shift down.

FIXME: Speed, Burrow Speed, Climb Speed, Fly Speed, Swim Speed.
FIXME: Terrain Types: Difficult Terrain, Hazardous Terrain, Narrow Surfaces, Uneven Ground, Inclines.
Zones of Control
When playing with TOTM the GM determines whether attacks of opportunity occur. When playing on a grid we need a more precise definition. We define a Zone of Control as the one square perimeter around the character, See Figurefigure:zones. The Ogre A is in character X's zone of control, Ogre B is not.
We suggest you use a scale where the length of one square in the grid corresponds to . This value is compatible with other TTRPGs and makes ranged combat sane approximately sane and consistent when converting from metric to imperial or vice versa.
Zones of Control figure:zones
Attacks of Opportunity
If characters or monsters move past opponents during combat they may grant an attack of opportunity which is a standard action made as an Out-of-Turn Action to the movement. Disengaging from combat and moving away from combat does not grant an attack of opportunity.
A character grants an Attack of Opportunity every time the they move from one cell in an opponents zone of control into another cell in any opponents zone of control. The attack of opportunity is granted to the opponent whose cell the character moves to. In Figurefigure:opportunity_attack_simple, monster A gives attacks of opportunity whenever he moves along the arrows in the diagram.
When a moving creature is hit by an Attack of Opportunity that movement action ends.
Simple Attacks of Opportunity figure:opportunity_attacks_simple
Complex Attacks of Opportunity figure:opportunity_attacks_complex
Reach
Reach Reach weapons, such as spears, are melee weapons with a longer range than most. Weapons with reach have the advantage that they grant an Opportunity Attack when an opponent moves into a characters zone of control. For example, in Figurefigure:reach_weapons, Ogre A gives an attack of opportunity to Character P whenever he moves along the arrows in the diagram if character P is wielding a weapon with the Reach keyword.
Reach Weapons figure:reach_weapons
Flanking sec:flanking
When playing using theatre of the mind, whether or not a character is flanked is determined by role-playing and GM fiat, the GM might require the character makes a check to leap over a table to get into a flanking position.
When playing on a grid a defender is said to be Flanked if he within reach of two or more opponents capable of making melee attacks on the defender, and the angle from the center of the first attacker to the center of the defender, then to the center of the second attacker forms an angle of greater than 90° degrees. Attacks on flanked characters are shifted up, gain a +2 check modifier, see Figurefigure:flanking
Flanked
A defender is Flanked when the angle between any two melee attackers is greater than 90° degrees. Flanked characters grant a shift up to all attackers.
Flanking Examples figure:flanking
Formation
It is possible to fight in Formation. While fighting in a formation the front row provides hard cover to the back row ( two shifts up to second row defence counterchecks). The front row must have at least as many people in it as the back row. To make melee attacks from the back row you must be using a weapon with reach. It is possible for a group to have two front rows, to be fighting on two fronts, provided that the number of people in each front row is greater than or equal to the number of people in the back row.
Formation Examples figure:formation
Creature Sizes
Monsters come in varying sizes. Humans, Dwarves and Elves are considered medium, Halflings are Small. Cats, Chickens and Tiny. Horses are Large. Elephants are Huge and Dragons are Gargantuan.
Sizes, Monster
Monster sizes range from Tiny, Small, Medium, Large, Huge and Gargantuan. Humans are Medium, Cats are Tiny, and Elephants are Large.
Tiny
A monster size as large as a cat, a chicken, or a small dog.
Small
A monster size as large as a child, a halfling, or a large dog.
Medium
A monster size as large as an adult human, dwarf or elf.
Large
A monster size as larg e as a horse or cow.
Huge
A monster size as large as an elephant.
Gargantuan
A monster size much larger than an elephant, a dragon.

section.sectiontitle:
Non-Lethal Combat sec:non-lethal-combat
Combat Non-Lethal Combat
section.p: There are two categories of combat: Lethal and Non-Lethal. In Non-Lethal combat the participants are not actively trying to kill their opponents, but rather trying to subdue them or drive them off.

There is no difference between Lethal and Non-Lethal combat until an opponents stamina reaches zero and someone becomes Bloodied. At that point a decision has to be made as to whether the combat is lethal or non-lethal. If the combat is non-lethal then the bloodied opponent has to willingly withdraw from the combat or make a morale check to convert the combat to a Lethal Combat. So it is possibly for a non-lethal combat to become lethal at some point during the combat. Ultimately the GM decides what type of combat is occurring, but as a guide combat between civilized humanoids, particularly in places with established legal systems and prohibitions against violence, will be assumed to be non-lethal, at least initially. Combat against monsters and uncivilized humanoids should be considered to be lethal be default.

There is a case where, during a non-lethal combat, a character may have lost most of their stamina, and are then hit with a big hit and lose all their remaining health. In such a case the normal rules for reduction of health to zero apply. This will probably result in either the combat becoming lethal, or the opponents running away. Weapons with the non-lethal keyword reduce the opponents health to one in this case.

Examples of typical non-lethal combat encounters include fights with the local guards, bar-room brawls, fights with gangs of thugs and bandits. There are many reasons to use non-lethal combat: killing people is often a capital crime in human society, there are severe social implications when an individual becomes known as a killer, potentially the players might wish to interrogate an opponent, and bandits might want to make money selling people into slavery.

section.p: Refreshes SleepHealing RestHealing Healing Characters may heal by taking a long or a short rest. A Short Rest is a ten minute or more length of time that the characters perform no strenuous activity. At the end of a short rest the characters regain all their Stamina and may refresh one dice pool at their dice pool refresh rate.

A Long Rest is a six hour or more length of time that the characters sleep. At the end of a long rest the characters regain all their Stamina, regain Health at their Health Heal rate, and refresh dice into their dice pools at twice their dice pool refresh rate. Previously unused short rests can be taken at the same time as a long rest.

NPCs and monsters behave differently from PCs during combat in the following ways:
PCs should automatically win initiative under normal circumstances.
Groups of NPCs and Monsters often share a Mettle Pool.

descriptions.description: Counter Attack counter-attack The character gains an immediate standard melee action as a free action.

Friendly Fire friendly-fire The character shooting a ranged weapon into melee strikes an ally in that melee. If there are no allies in the melee the target is involved in, then the attack simply misses. If there are more than one ally in the melee then one ally is targeted randomly. The ally may make a defensive reaction if they have a Out-of-Turn Action available.
